analytic.title: Estimating Sex-Specific Abundance in Fawning Areas of a High-Density Columbian Black-Tailed Deer Population Using Fecal DNA

div.p: The recent development of fecal-genetic capture-mark-recapture (CMR) methods has increased the feasibility of estimating abundance of forest-dwelling ungulates that are difficult to survey using visual methods. Unless genetic markers differentiating sex are incorporated into such studies, however, genetic CMR approaches risk missing sex-specific differences in population trends. We developed a singlereaction genetic assay for sex and individual identification, including 10 microsatellites and an SRY marker, and applied it in the context of a post-fawning CMR study of Columbian black-tailed deer (Odocoileus hemionus columbianus) in forested habitat of coastal California during 2011 and 2012. We measured sexspecific abundance and sex ratios in high-quality summer habitats encompassing 4 distinct fawning areas. We detected a significant interaction between sex and year, indicating different trends in the abundance of males and females. We also detected a significant decline in abundance of females between years (P ¼ 0.045), which agreed with independent telemetry-based estimates, and significant differences in female abundance among fawning areas (P ¼ 0.020) but no significant differences in the abundance of males for either variable (F 1-3,20 < 0.710, P > 0.410). When sex was not considered in the analysis, we found no significant differences in abundance between the 2 years, suggesting that differing trends between the 2 sexes obscured the femalespecific patterns. We estimated average local (i.e., on the high-quality summer ranges) density ( D) for females at 41.0 (AE 5.9) deer/km 2 in 2011 and 29.1 (AE 6.8) deer/km 2 in 2012, and local density of males at 15.7 (AE 3.0) deer/km 2 across the 2 study years. Accordingly, sex ratios differed between years (95% CI ¼ 3.0-4.2 F:M ratio in 2011, 2.0-2.3 F:M ratio in 2012). Incorporating sex and individual markers into a single assay provided a cost-effective means of applying CMR estimation based on fecal DNA to a high-density ungulate population in a forested ecosystem and emphasized the importance of explicitly modeling sex in abundance estimation.

the relative importance of top-down versus bottom-up factors affecting population growth rates, which requires information on population abundance (and habitat quality), is fundamental to effective management of ungulate populations (Morellet et al. 2007, Pierce et al. 2012b, Monteith et al. 2014).

Management of ungulate populations also requires an understanding of their demographic composition at any given point in time and potential differences in population trends between sexes (McCullough 1999). Female abundance and trends are particularly important determinants of overall population growth (Gaillard et al. 2000). Because male and female ungulates exhibit different life histories, home range sizes, habitat use patterns, and cause-specific mortality rates, including differential harvest rates from hunting, sex-specific relative abundance estimates are especially valuable (Connolly 1981, Geist 1981, Ebert et al. 2012).

Most traditional approaches to monitoring abundance and composition of ungulate populations involve use of distance sampling through aerial counts or other means, indices (e.g., sign counts, relative abundance counts) or, more recently, capture-mark-recapture (CMR) approaches (Mowat andStrobeck 2000, Acevedo et al. 2008). Each methodology has significant downsides that limit its value or feasibility. Aerial transect counts are expensive, can be hazardous, and unless corrected for sightability using marked individuals (e.g., Wittmer et al. 2005) typically result in imprecise estimates of abundance (Caughley 1974, Bartmann et al. 1986). Aerial surveys also are less feasible in forested habitats where trees obscure sight. Indirect approaches (e.g., pellet deposition counts) yield less accurate correlates of abundance (Fuller 1991) that are less amenable to comparisons among study sites (Morellet et al. 2007). Estimating accurate sex ratios from count surveys also is difficult because of biases associated with differential behavior and microhabitat use of males and females (McCullough 1994) or an inability to differentiate young, antlerless males from females (Wittmer et al. 2005). The CMR methods on the other hand provide statistically robust abundance estimates but involve costly, often invasive capture procedures and require large sample sizes to achieve a useful degree of precision (Pierce et al. 2012a).

The advent of molecular genetic techniques sensitive enough to obtain individual-specific genotypes from lowquantity DNA sources such as fecal pellets and hair has recently opened up promising avenues for adopting CMR approaches to noninvasive sampling schemes (Lukacs and Burnham 2005, Harris et al. 2010, Brinkman et al. 2011). Unique genotypes obtained from DNA in noninvasively collected fecal pellets or hair samples can be used to identify individuals upon initial capture (i.e., identification via DNA) and recapture, enabling the pellet or hair samples to take the place of physically marked individuals. Fecal DNA also can be used to accurately differentiate sexes (e.g., Brinkman andHundertmark 2009, Ebert et al. 2012) and assess sex ratios (e.g., before vs. after harvest; Pierce et al. 2012a). Lastly, the genotypic data generated in such approaches can be used for additional purposes, such as to evaluate genetic diversity or familial relationships (Waits and Paetkau 2005, Yoshizaki 2007, Colson et al. 2013).

Here, we describe a sex-specific CMR study of a Columbian black-tailed deer (Odocoileus hemionus columbianus) population in northern California. The genetic diversity of these deer is among the highest of the species, suggesting correspondingly high density (Latch et al. 2014). Previous studies demonstrated the utility of CMR methods for sexagnostic abundance estimation in low-density deer populations (e.g., Brinkman et al. 2011). The application of CMR approaches to a high-density population affords the advantage of facilitating larger samples sizes and, therefore, the greater feasibility to obtain sex-specific estimates of abundance. On the other hand, larger samples sizes also entail greater expense, necessitating efficiencies to reduce per-sample costs. Therefore, we developed a single DNA-based assay composed of 11 markers to simultaneously estimate sex and individual, which we applied in a CMR framework to estimate the relative abundances of male and female deer among 4 separate fawning areas over 2 years. Specific objectives were to 1) estimate deer abundance from fecal samples collected from 4 summer-range fawning areas within a 150-km 2 area using discrete CMR models, 2) estimate sex ratios using direct (sex-specific pellet counts) and indirect (sex-specific abundance estimates) approaches, and 3) compare these metrics over time and space to explore the potential for this approach to detect spatiotemporal heterogeneity. Lastly, we evaluated these results in the context of demographic parameters estimated during a concurrent 4-year telemetry study based on 136 fawns and 57 females older than 1 year of age from the same population (Marescot et al. 2015).

div.head: STUDY AREA
div.p: We conducted our study in the Mendocino National Forest in northern California, USA (Fig. 1). The topography is mountainous with elevations ranging from approximately 400 m to 2,000 m. Climate is considered Mediterranean with generally mild winter temperatures. Average annual precipitation was 132 cm, the majority of which occurred between December and March. Below 1,000 m, winter precipitation was predominantly in the form of rain. During summers, there is little precipitation and humidity is low, which are ideal conditions for DNA preservation on fecal pellets. A detailed description of the vegetation communities can be found in Allen et al. (2014). Black-tailed deer are the only ungulate species traditionally occurring in the study area. Although a recent study reported mule-deer introgression in some northern California Columbian blacktailed deer populations (Latch et al. 2014), we found no evidence of substantial mule deer ancestry in this population based either on morphological characteristics or on sequencing of mitochondrial D-loop DNA (J. L. Brazeal, University of California, unpublished data). Specifically, comparison of sequences (450 bp) from 49 deer captured in the study area (Marescot et al. 2015) all matched or clustered with previously published Columbian black-tailed deer haplotypes and none with continental mule deer haplotypes (Latch et al. 2009;J. L. Brazeal, unpublished data).

div.head: METHODS
div.p: The area over which we collected deer pellets extended approximately 150 km 2 and encompassed 4 areas of high quality deer summer habitat. Female deer concentrated in these high quality habitats to give birth and so we refer to them as fawning areas (Cold Spring, Plaskett Meadow, Coyote Rock, and Cherry Hill/Tar Flat; Fig. 1). In each of the 4 distinct fawning areas, we defined a 20-km 2 (5 Â 4 km) sample plot covering a range of elevations including summer habitat used by both sexes. Within each sample plot, we established 4-6 (2011) or 6 (2012) 1.2-km long, 2-m wide belt transects (14,400 m 2 total area), each of which began at a random point in the plot and followed deer trails (when present) that were closest to a random compass bearing, similarly to a previous study of Sitka black-tailed deer (O. h. sitkensis) by Brinkman et al. (2011). We ensured that no portion of any transect was <1.5 km from any other transect; this minimum distance was greater than the average diameter of an adult female home range (McCorquodale 1999, Forrester 2014), ensuring that each transect was an independent sample unit.

For practical reasons associated with a companion study (Marescot et al. 2015), the seasonal timing of our sampling occurred after the birth of fawns each year, such that our abundance and sex ratio estimates included fawns. We sampled transects twice during 2011 (22 Aug-23 Sep) and 4 times during 2012 (16 Jul-19 Sep), with each sampling event separated by 7-10 days in both years. Because of a forest fire, 2 transects in 2012 had to be relocated after the first sampling period and were thus sampled only 3 times. On the first sampling occasion, we collected fresh pellets with a mucous sheen and attempted to clear all pellets from within the 2-m transect, as well as 1 m beyond the boundary on either side. During subsequent surveys, we collected pellets from all groups, presumably deposited since the previous sampling occasion, and cleared remaining pellets from 1-2 m beyond either side. For each pellet group, we recorded the date, time, global positioning system (GPS) waypoint, and habitat description. We collected 4-6 pellets from each pellet group in a tube containing 95-100% ethanol and transferred them to the Mammalian Ecology and Conservation Unit of the University of California Davis Veterinary Genetics Laboratory for processing.

div.head: DNA Analysis
div.p: We developed an assay for fecal genotyping that included 10 microsatellites and 1 sex-typing marker (a highly conserved portion of the SRY gene on the Y chromosome for sex determination; Table 1). We selected these markers from 24 previously published loci (22 microsatellites, 2 sex markers) originally developed for a variety of ruminants on the basis of their performance on both tissue and fecal DNA (Olegario 2013). To characterize parameters (e.g., polymorphism, sexspecificity) of the 11 selected markers in the present population, we used DNA extracted from ear-punch tissue samples collected from 32 individuals (25 adult females, 7 male fawns) during captures for a concurrent study (Marescot et al. 2015). We extracted DNA from deer tissue using the Qiagen DNeasy Blood and Tissue Kit (Qiagen, Valencia, CA) as per manufacturers protocols. We extracted DNA from the surfaces of fecal pellets in batches of 11 samples with 1 blank as a negative control to assess possible contamination following a protocol modified from Brinkman et al. (2010). We first dried 2 to 4 pellets at 21 8C for 45 minutes to remove residual ethanol. Next, we washed the outside of the pellets in sterile 20-ml scintillation vials with 1 ml to 1.5 ml buffer ATL (Qiagen) for 1 hour. We then used the Qiagen DNeasy Blood and Tissue Kit according to manufacturer protocols for blood to extract DNA from the resulting suspension of epithelial cells. We amplified microsatellite markers and the sex marker using polymerase chain reaction (PCR) with a Qiagen multiplex PCR kit (Qiagen). The PCR mixtures contained 1 ml genomic DNA extract, 0.5 ml RNase-free water, 5.0 ml Qiagen Multiplex Mastermix, 1.0 ml Q-solution, and 2.5 ml primer mixture (Table 1). We amplified DNA using a thermal profile consisting of a 15-minute denaturing step at 95 8C followed by 33 cycles combining a 30-second denaturation step at 94 8C, a 1.5-minute annealing step at 58 8C, and a 1-minute extension step at 72 8C followed by a final extension step for 10 minutes at 72 8C. We genotyped samples using an ABI 3730 (Applied Biosystems, Grand Island, NY) and internal size standards (500-LIZ; Applied Biosystems). We manually scored alleles using electropherograms visualized in Program STRand (version 2.4.89), which provisionally bins DNA fragments into discrete size categories (i.e., alleles) relative to the internal size standards (Toonen and Hughes 2001).

Using the 32 high-quality (tissue) DNA samples, we estimated the average number of alleles per locus (N A ), observed heterozygosity (H O ), expected heterozygosity (H E ), and polymorphic informative content (PIC) using Microsatellite Toolkit (Park 2001). We assessed departures from Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium (HWE) and linkage disequilibrium (LD) using Arlequin Version 3.5 (Excoffier and Lischer 2010). We corrected for multiple comparisons using the sequential Bonferroni correction (Rice 1989). We calculated the probability of identity (P ID ) and, more conservatively, probability of identity for siblings (P ID Sibs) for our loci and the entire multilocus assay (Paetkau andStrobeck 1994, Waits et al. 2001). We also used the average locus-specific P ID and P ID Sibs estimates to calculate probabilities of agreement at 9 loci, 8 loci, 7 loci, etc. Specifically, we used the following probability calculations:

The DNA extracted from fecal pellets is typically low quantity and fragmented, necessitating replicate PCRs to reduce rates of allelic dropout in composite genotypes (Bonin et al. 2004). We randomly selected a subset of DNA samples to estimate allelic dropout and false allele rates. We conducted 4 independent PCRs and electrophoresis runs, and genotyped each sample blindly. We excluded from the analysis samples that did not successfully amplify !9 loci in any of the runs. For each of the 47 remaining samples, we produced a composite genotype based on all 4 replicates, and estimated allelic dropout and false alleles based on comparison of individual replicates to composite genotypes (Bonin et al. 2004, Pompanon et al. 2005). Specifically, we identified each of the 470 locus-samples (i.e., 47 samples Â 10 loci) as a heterozygote or homozygote. We then estimated the allelic dropout rate as the proportion of replicate genotypes corresponding to heterozygous locussamples that were homozygous in state. Tentative false alleles were identified when more than 2 alleles were present among the 4 replicates or as an allele unique to a single replicate when the other 3 replicates were homozygous for a different allele. Although we did not find any, we would have confirmed tentative false alleles through additional replications. These estimates represented average per-replicate error rates across all loci. For all other samples in this study, we used a minimum of 2 replicates to form a composite genotype for each sample (see below). Therefore, we squared the per-replicate error frequencies to obtain the minimum expected composite-genotype error frequencies.

Based on the allelic dropout rates estimated in the previous step, we devised a protocol to optimize replication effort. We initially genotyped all samples twice using independent PCRs and based further replication on their quality. Specifically, we considered those samples yielding highquality genotypes (i.e., successful amplification at !7 loci and all loci represented in at least 1 replicate) to be complete based on the 2 replicates. We replicated moderate to lowquality genotypes (first 2 replicates amplifying 4-6 loci with some peak heights higher than standards) up to 5 additional times (for a total of 3-7 replicates) and excluded genotypes with !1 locus missing from composite genotypes from further analyses. We combined replicates into composite genotypes (i.e., 1 per fecal sample) for downstream analyses by assigning any allele that occurred in at least 1 replicate to the composite genotype in Program Gimlet (Valie `re 2002). Any genotyping error remaining after replication and integration into the final composite genotype would result in the possibility that 2 samples from the same individual could have non-identical genotypes (Creel et al. 2003). Conversely, 2 distinct individuals could share the same genotype by chance, with probabilities depending on the polymorphism of our loci (i.e, shadow effect; Mills et al. 2000). Each of these problems would cause biases in downstream abundance estimation. Therefore, we accounted for these potential sources of error by selecting thresholds to minimize or eliminate them (McKelvey and Schwartz 2004). We used the match probabilities described above (eq 1) to select an upper limit of genotype match agreement expected between 2 distinct individuals and used genotyping error frequencies to estimate the lower limit of match agreement expected from 2 genotypes from the same individual. We chose a threshold number of mismatches to distinguish same versus different individuals that would minimize both types of error: incorrectly assigning different (i.e., imperfect) genotypes from the same individual to multiple individuals or failing to distinguish distinct individuals. We then used a pairwise genotype-matching analysis performed in the AlleleMatch package in R to assign composite genotypes to unique individuals based on this estimated maximum threshold number of mismatching loci (Galpern et al. 2012, R Core Team 2012).

div.head: Population Abundance Estimates
div.p: Because fawn mortality was non-negligible during the sampling periods (Marescot et al. 2015), ours was not in fact a closed population during the survey. Nevertheless, for purposes of analysis, we tested models that assumed a closed population within sample years because such models have fewer parameters and we expected that our sampling periods were sufficiently brief to minimize confounding effects of deaths. We estimated abundance ( N ) for each transect in each year using the Huggins closed capture models in Program MARK (Huggins 1989, White andBurnham 1999), and evaluated whether violations of the populationclosure assumption were statistically detectable. Specifically, we compared the closed-population model to the openpopulation Jolly-Seber model in CloseTest version 3 (Stanley andBurnham 1999, Stanley andRichards 2005). We applied a sequential Bonferroni correction to guard against inflated type I errors associated with multiple comparisons (Rice 1989). Because we sampled transects 4 times in 2012 and only twice in 2011, we had both more reason to expect violations of closure and sufficient statistical power to test the assumptions of closure in 2012. Therefore, we performed tests (for each transect) in 2012, reasoning that if it was not a statistical problem in this year, it likely was not in 2011 either. Along with population closure, we assumed that capture and recapture probability were equivalent because our noninvasive sampling technique was unlikely to affect pellet deposition by deer. Because we sampled only pellets with a mucous sheen (i.e., recently deposited pellets) on the first capture occasion, we assumed that our initial captures were within approximately the same post-deposition timeframe as our recaptures. Thus, to minimize the use of unnecessary parameters, our model included constant capture probability (p) equal to recapture probability (c) for the entire study area. For each year, we combined all encounter histories into a single input file and treated transects as unique groups to estimate p and transect-specific N . We considered multiple captures of the same individual within a sampling occasion a single capture event. We never sampled the same individual on multiple transects in a single sampling occasion. For each transect, we estimated both sexagnostic and sex-specific N . We excluded 2 transects that were affected by the forest fire in 2012 from the Huggins models because they were sampled only 3 times.

Calculation of density estimates from abundance estimates adds another level of uncertainty, in particular uncertainty associated with assumptions about the effective area sampled. Nevertheless, for comparative purposes it can be useful to calculate such estimates with the explicit understanding that they are meaningful only within the context of similarly calculated estimates. Therefore, to convert our abundance estimates to local density estimates ( D), we divided N by the estimated effective area represented by the transect (A ˆ; Parmenter et al. 2003), which we calculated similarly to Brinkman et al. (2011). First, we determined the maximum distance between any 2 samples for each resampled individual. Second, we estimated the median among these individual maximum distances-the median maximum recapture distance (MMRD). Third, we created a buffer beyond the original 2-m wide by 1.2-km long transects equal to the MMRD and used the resulting buffered area as our estimate of A ˆ. To assess abundance differences by sex, year, and fawning area, we compared 2 quantities as dependent variables reflecting abundance: the raw estimates of numbers of individuals sampled (i.e., minimum numbers) and the CMR estimates of abundance ( N ). We treated transects as the sample units and compiled data and estimates for each sex, year, and fawning area separately. To assess interactions, we applied a fully factorial, 2-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) for each dependent variable with sex (F, M), year (2011,2012), and fawning area (Cold Spring, Plaskett Meadow, Coyote Rock, and Cherry Hill/Tar Flat) as the independent variables (Zar 1984). Because sampling occasions differed between years, we also conducted a parallel set of analyses based solely on the first 2 transect checks in 2012 to achieve a balanced design. We found no qualitative differences between these analyses and those based on the full data set and therefore present only the latter results. We estimated sex ratios based both on numbers of individuals genotyped and CMR estimates of abundance. To obtain confidence intervals on sex ratio estimates, we expressed them as proportions of samples that were female, estimated 95% confidence limits for these proportions based on the relationship between the F and binomial distributions (Zar 1984), and then back-transformed confidence limits to ratios [i.e., 1/(1 À p)].

div.head: DNA Analysis
div.p: We estimated the genetic diversity statistics corresponding to the 10 microsatellite markers based on the 32 high-quality deer tissue samples (Table 2). We found no significant linkage disequilibrium, but 2 loci deviated significantly from Hardy-Weinberg Equilibrium, CERVID1 and SBTD05, possibly indicating null alleles. As expected, all 7 males were positive for the SRY (Y-chromosome) marker and were hemizygous for the X-linked CELB9 marker, and all 25 females were negative for the SRY locus and were heterozygous or homozygous for the CELB9 locus, consistent with expected inheritance patterns for these sex-linked markers. We calculated the P ID and P ID Sibs conservatively using only the 7 (of 10) microsatellite loci remaining after excluding the X-linked locus and the 2 loci potentially containing null alleles (Table 2). These estimates indicated a negligible probability (<10 À7 ) that 2 randomly selected deer would share identical genotypes and a 1 in 500 chance that 2 siblings would share the same genotype at these 7 loci. The high polymorphism of the 3 additional microsatellite loci (i.e., with X-linkage or possible null alleles) along with the sex-marker increased the resolving power of this assay well beyond these estimates. Based on the conservative P ID and P ID Sibs estimates, this suite of loci should result in essentially all randomly paired individuals (and 98% of siblings) sharing no more than 7 of their 10 loci (Fig. 2). We collected 1,540 pellet samples during our 2-year sampling period. Of these, 1,016 (66%) pellet samples yielded genotypes with !7 microsatellite loci, and 760 (49%) yielded genotypes with all 10 microsatellite loci (Fig. 3). Based on a subsample of 47 samples successfully genotyped 4 times and which yielded !9 amplified loci in 1 or more of the genotypes, we observed allelic dropouts in 1.8% of locusreplicates and no false alleles. This per-replicate error rate corresponded to an estimated allelic dropout rate of 0.03% in genotypes composed from 2 replicates and implied a probability >99.6% that 2 10-locus genotypes of the same individual would agree at !9 loci. Therefore, we chose as our threshold 2 locus mismatches, at or below which genotypes were considered to derive from the same individual and above which genotypes were considered to derive from distinct individuals. We also confirmed that all mismatches could be explained solely by allelic dropout. Empirically, plotting all pairwise differences of numbers of mismatches among all 10locus composite genotypes used in this study revealed a clear bimodal distribution with all comparisons differing either by >3 or <3 loci, but almost never by exactly 3 loci (Fig. 4). Thus, the suite of loci in the assay appeared sufficient to ensure unambiguous assignment of distinct genotypes to the same or different individuals with high confidence.

div.head: Population Abundance Indexes and Estimates
div.p: Of the 760 pellet samples that yielded full genotypes, we identified 404 unique individuals, 9 of which were represented in both years (Fig. 3). The overall sex ratio in numbers of individuals sampled was 2.72 F:M (95% CI ¼ 2.15-3.47), which differed between 2011 (3.68, 95% CI ¼ 2.94-4.74) and 2012 (2.27, 95% CI ¼ 2.05-2.53). Capture probability (p) estimates were similar for females and males but generally higher in 2011 (p F ¼ 0.35, 95% CI ¼ 0.25-0.46; p M ¼ 0.32, 95% CI ¼ 0.17-0.54) than in 2012 (p F ¼ 0.22, 95% CI ¼ 0.18-0.26; p M ¼ 0.19, 95% CI ¼ 0.14-0.27). For most transects in 2012, our Stanley and Burnham Closure Test revealed no significant violations of model assumptions among all transects (P ! 0.25). However, Plaskett Meadows showed significant violation of closure (P ¼ 0.002) due to apparent additions during Table 2. To test if our model was robust to this violation, we performed and compared CMR analyses based only on the first 2 encounter histories to those based only on the last 2 encounter histories in 2012 (i.e., 2 shorter, independent measurements of the same transect). A paired t-test among the 6 Plaskett Meadow transects indicated no significant difference in the estimates (t 5 ¼ 0.70, P ¼ 0.41) and the 2 estimates were highly correlated among transects (r ¼ 0.98). Thus, estimates of N were apparently robust to the violations of the closure assumption.

div.head: Locus
div.p: Analysis of Huggins model estimates of abundance indicated a significant interaction between sex and year (F 1-3,60 ¼ 3.99, P ¼ 0.05), suggesting that sex ratios differed in the 2 years (Figs. 5 and6). We found no significant 3-way interaction or interactions between year and fawning area or between sex and fawning area (F 1-3,50 <1.09, P > 0.36). The follow-up ANOVAs conducted separately on sexes indicated significant differences between years (F 1,30 ¼ 4.37, P ¼ 0.045) and among fawning areas (F 3,30 ¼ 3.83, P ¼ 0.020) for females but no significant differences among the estimates of abundance of males (F 1- 3,20 <0.71, P > 0.41; Table 3). We estimated an MMRD of 126 m based on all individuals sampled more than once in the study (n ¼ 196 individuals), giving us an estimated effective area A ˆ¼ 0.35 km 2 per transect. We used this estimate to convert abundance estimates to per-transect density indices, which we could then average across fawning areas. In 2011, D ranged from 7.80 (AE SE ¼ 2.60) M/km 2 to 18.20 (AE 6.88) M/km 2 and from 24.58 (AE 3.48) F/km 2 to 52.45 (AE 10.75) F/km 2 . In 2012, D ranged from 11.40 (AE 3.26) M/km 2 to 26.38 (AE 12.22) M/km 2 and from 14.36 (AE 3.40) F/km 2 to 41.58 (AE 9.83) F/km 2 across fawning areas.

The average abundance (and density) estimates in the 4 fawning areas were highly correlated with the numbers of individuals sampled, both for females (r ¼ 0.98) and males (r > 0.99). Similarly, the numbers of females were highly correlated with numbers of males across fawning areas, both in terms of numbers of individuals sampled (r ¼ 0.91) and abundance estimates (r ¼ 0.88). Thus, changes in sex ratios detected between the 2 years appear to have affected all fawning areas similarly.

For comparison to our sex-specific estimates of abundance, we also estimated abundance of deer irrespective of sex (i.e., pooling capture histories of F and M) to assess how this would affect statistical resolution. In general, the estimates for each fawning area in the 2 years were similar to those obtained by summing the separate female and male estimates. The ANOVA detected similar differences among fawning areas (F 3,31 ¼ 3.42, P ¼ 0.029) as detected for females above. However, we detected no difference between years (F 1,31 ¼ 0.57, P ¼ 0.46), suggesting that the different trends in females and males obscured the difference in female abundance discovered in the sex-specific analysis.

div.head: DISCUSSION
div.p: We successfully used fecal DNA analyzed in a single assay to estimate site-specific abundance within a high-density deer population with sufficient precision to detect differences in space, time, and sexes. Explicit incorporation of sex in our study proved especially important, enabling us to observe sex-specific differences in abundance and, consequently, to detect trends in the female segment of the population that would otherwise have been missed. In particular, we detected a decline in females between years that was not evident in our analysis that ignored sex (or of males alone). The declining trend in female abundance observed in the present study was supported by results from a contemporaneous study that used population-specific estimates of fecundity, fawn survival, and adult female survival to estimate population growth based on a Leslie matrix. Resulting estimates of population growth (l) averaged 0.82 (SD ¼ 0.13) over the 4-year period data were collected (i.e., May 2009 to Aug 2013; Marescot et al. 2015). Differences in fawn survival detected in the telemetry study varied tremendously within fawning areas from 1 season or year to the next (e.g., ranging 0.10 to 0.99), precluding direct comparisons with our fawning area-specific abundance estimates. Nevertheless, fawning area also was found to be a significant factor underlying differences in fawn survival probabilities (Forrester 2014, Marescot et al. 2015), in qualitative agreement with the heterogeneity in spatial abundance observed in the present noninvasive CMR study. An important finding of the genetic CMR data beyond that obtained from the telemetry study of adult females and fawns was the lack of detectable spatial and temporal variation in population densities and trends of adult males. Black-tailed deer in the Mendocino National Forest, similarly to other deer populations across much of the United States, were subjected to male-only harvest, such that hunting was potentially the most important mortality source specific to adult males. Moreover, males of polygamous ungulate species tend to have lower survival than females in general (Gaillard et al. 2000). Thus, it is not surprising that we found lower density estimates for males than females. The lower overall density of males and, therefore, smaller sample size, however, also reduced our statistical power to detect spatial differences in males and females. Thus, although the significant interaction between sex and year provided strong support for the observed differences in temporal trends between the sexes, it is unclear whether males and females differed in their spatial distribution over the sampling area.

Population parameters derived from CMR models using noninvasive DNA samples are especially useful in management applications because they are readily comparable across years. These estimates can also be estimated at multiple spatial scales such as seasonal ranges or landscape scales (Brinkman et al. 2011). However, density estimates must be interpreted in the context of the particular study design and not extrapolated beyond the appropriate spatial scale or season. Our study was designed to estimate local abundance in high-quality habitats that were used only during summer following seasonal migrations of deer to higher elevations (Allen et al. 2014) and specifically after fawning, when abundance would be at its annual peak. Because our transect placement was random within preselected fawning areas, our estimates were applicable only to these approximately 20km 2 areas. Extrapolation of our estimates to larger spatial scales, such as over the entire Mendocino National Forest, would likely constitute a significant overestimate if the larger region included patches that were relatively devoid of deer during summer. Additionally, given the average number of fawns birthed per female (1.9), as well as annual mortality of fawns (0.76, most of which occurred from mid-Jun to mid-Sep) and adult females (0.29; Marescot et al. 2015), our postfawning abundance estimates could have been as much as 3 times higher than pre-fawning abundance estimates. Importantly, however, the lack of interaction observed in the present study between temporal trend and spatial heterogeneity indicates that sampling of the same summer ranges across multiple years can provide robust trend data for long-term monitoring.

The assay developed for this study presents a technological advance that can be applied broadly to similar CMR studies of deer and other ruminants. Previous research aimed at developing fecal-DNA CMR approaches for ungulates has provided useful guidelines for field sampling and standards for data accuracy and resolution (e.g., Harris et al. 2010, Brinkman et al. 2011, Goode 2011). Our study built upon and added to these advances in 2 important ways: introduction of a high-efficiency fecal DNA assay and its incorporation of a sex marker, which enabled us to explicitly model each sex independently.

By incorporating 10 microsatellites and a sex marker (i.e., 11 markers) in a single reaction, our assay enabled us to simultaneously minimize error and cost, representing a significant improvement over previous assays. Although we used fewer reactions per sample than previous studies, our proportional success was similar to that observed in previous genetic CMR studies for which samples were genotyped up to 7 times or more (Brinkman et al. 2011, Goode 2011, Ebert et al. 2012). In contrast to previous studies, which either did not incorporate sex markers (or sex) in analyses (Brinkman et al. 2011) or conducted additional assays specifically to determine sex (Goode 2011, Ebert et al. 2012), our incorporation of a sex marker in the same assay used to determine individual genotypes further reduced the number of reactions required. Overall, our error rates were low (e.g., 1.8% allelic dropout vs. approx. 5% in other studies) and polymorphism high (e.g., P ID ¼ 10 À7 vs. up to 0.0003) relative to other studies (e.g., Brinkman et al. 2011, Ebert et al. 2012), although the high polymorphism of our panel was likely due in part to the relatively high genetic diversity in our population (Latch et al. 2014).

div.head: MANAGEMENT IMPLICATIONS
div.p: Our particular noninvasive genetic CMR approach allowed us to efficiently quantify 2 important population parameters, sex-specific abundance and sex ratio, in a high-density population of Columbian black-tailed deer inhabiting a forested landscape. These methods proved capable of capturing short-term trends within relatively small, highquality habitat areas that are known to be critical for fawn recruitment (Forrester 2014). We also detected an independently verified (Marescot et al. 2015) short-term decline in the female population that methods agnostic to sex would not have detected. Application of these methods in the future can provide information on sex-specific trends that can be compared to predictions of density-dependent models (Eberhardt 2002) and applied in conjunction with vital rate estimates to assess the relative importance of top-down and bottom-up factors affecting population dynamics (Pierce et al. 2012b). Such information can facilitate decisions about how best to manage populations with respect to harvest rates, predator populations, and habitat. Because the assay used in our study of Columbian black-tailed deer incorporated markers derived from a broad taxonomic range of ungulates including Cervidae and Bovidae, our assay should be broadly applicable to many managed and unmanaged ungulate species.
